wheel16k.title: The wheel at 16,000 samples per second
wheel16k.caption: On the wideband side a tone turns 360° × tone ÷ 16,000 per sample, so 4,000 Hz is a quarter turn. The filter should pass the top-right quarter and remove the top-left.

cutoff.title: The filter we want: a step
cutoff.caption: The wanted response: keep everything below 4,000 Hz whole, remove everything above. The cutoff sits halfway down the cliff.

fir.title: An FIR filter answers a click with its coefficients
fir.caption: With no feedback, a click comes out as the coefficient list, one number per sample, and then it stops. These five numbers are only an example.

ideal.title: The ideal low-pass’s coefficients never end
ideal.caption: The ideal list runs both ways from the middle and never ends. It produces the perfect step.

truncation.title: Cutting the list: the 0 Hz gain overshoots and settles
truncation.caption: Each pair of coefficients adds a step. The total overshoots to 1.1366, dives, and swings around 1, ending at 0.9802 with 31 kept.

pair-cosine.title: A pair of equal coefficients makes a flat number
pair-cosine.caption: Coefficient h[m] sees the arrow turned back m steps, h[−m] the arrow turned forward. Their sum is flat: 2 h[m] cos(m × turn). At 90°, as for 4,000 Hz with odd m, it is zero.

pair-bars.title: A negative gain, built from its parts
pair-bars.caption: At 4,500 Hz every pair pulls the gain down, and together they land on −0.090: 9% of the tone gets out, upside down.

sweep-ghost.title: The sweep and its ghost, in time
sweep-ghost.caption: The rising sweep comes out as a falling ghost that swells and vanishes every 500 Hz or so, deep inside the voice band.

gibbs.title: Longer cuts: the bump narrows, its height stays
gibbs.caption: More coefficients squeeze the ripple toward the cliff, but every bump still reaches 1.09.

decibels.title: Percent and decibels
decibels.caption: Each factor of ten is 20 dB. The Gibbs leak, 9%, is about −21 dB; the target, 1%, is −40 dB.

wiggles.title: The curve is a sum of wiggles
wiggles.caption: Each coefficient pair sets the size of one wiggle. Three wiggles and the middle coefficient already lean toward the step.

average.title: Different wiggles average to zero
average.caption: Two different wiggles multiplied average to zero over all the tones; a wiggle times itself averages to one half.

gibbs-build.title: Adding pairs builds the cliff, and the overshoot stays
gibbs-build.caption: Each pair sharpens the cliff and moves the bump closer to it, but the bump never drops below about 1.09.

window.title: Truncation is multiplying by a rectangle
window.caption: Keeping 31 coefficients is the same as multiplying the ideal list by a rectangle of ones.

rect-response.title: A window has a response of its own
rect-response.caption: The rectangle’s sharp edges give its response side lobes; the first is −22% of the hump. Hamming’s soft edges leave a wider hump and almost no side lobes.

smear.title: Sliding the hump along the cliff
smear.caption: The cut filter’s gain at each tone is the share of the hump’s area still on the pass side. The rectangle’s left-out side lobes are worth −9%, so 109% remains.

spec.title: The honest job, and where each band lands
spec.caption: Anything above 4,600 Hz lands in the voice band and must go. The slope may live between 3,400 and 4,600 Hz, because it lands in the empty margin.

taper.title: The Hamming taper over the ideal list
taper.caption: Hamming barely touches the big middle coefficients and squashes the small outer ones.

transition-band.title: The transition band of the Hamming filter
transition-band.caption: Between 3,458 and 4,542 Hz the filter is neither within 1% of whole nor below 1%: that stretch is its transition band.

trade.title: The window trade: shape sets the ripple
trade.caption: Same length, different shape: the rectangle’s ripple sits near −21 dB, Hamming’s below −54 dB.

done.title: What done looks like
done.caption: Hamming, 45 coefficients: the voice band within 0.24%, the ghost below 0.24%, and the slope only in the margin.
